questions.question: Employers must auto-enrol eligible workers aged 22+ who earn over…
questions.explanation: The auto-enrolment earnings trigger is £10,000 a year.

questions.question: The minimum total auto-enrolment contribution on qualifying earnings is…
questions.explanation: 8% in total, with at least 3% from the employer.

questions.question: The minimum employer contribution under auto-enrolment is…
questions.explanation: Employers must pay at least 3% of qualifying earnings.

questions.question: Opting out of your workplace pension means…
questions.explanation: Opting out gives up money your employer would add for you.

questions.question: Pension tax relief means…
options: The government adds back tax on your contributions
questions.explanation: Contributions get tax relief at your income tax rate, within limits.

questions.question: The normal minimum age to access most private pensions is…
questions.explanation: The minimum pension age is set to rise to 57 in 2028.

questions.question: The State Pension age is 66 and is rising to…
questions.explanation: It's rising to 67 between 2026 and 2028.

questions.question: To get any new State Pension you usually need at least how many qualifying NI years?
questions.explanation: You usually need 10 years for any State Pension and 35 for the full amount.

questions.question: You invest £100 a month for 30 years at 5% a year. Roughly how much do you end up with?
questions.explanation: You pay in £36,000, and compound growth takes it to about £83,000.

questions.question: Most people can take up to what share of their pension tax-free?
questions.explanation: Usually 25%, subject to an overall cap.
questions.verify: Tax-free lump sum rules and cap

questions.question: Lost track of an old workplace pension? Use…
questions.explanation: It's free on gov.uk.

questions.question: Workplace pension auto-enrolment means:
options: You must save all your salary
Most employees are automatically enrolled into a pension, and can opt out
questions.explanation: Auto-enrolment puts you in unless you opt out; the default is designed to build you a pension.

questions.question: The minimum auto-enrolment contribution is around:
options: 8% of qualifying earnings total, with at least 3% from the employer
questions.explanation: The 8% minimum includes employer 3% and employee 5% (with tax relief); figures can change.

questions.question: Opting out of your workplace pension means losing:
options: Your employer's contributions and the tax relief, effectively free money
questions.explanation: Opting out saves money today but forfeits employer money and tax relief worth a lot over a career.

questions.question: Pension tax relief means:
options: The government adds back the tax you paid on contributions, boosting what's invested
Relief is only for the rich
questions.explanation: Basic-rate relief adds 25p for every £1 you contribute; higher earners can claim more.

questions.question: Your employer matches pension contributions. Not contributing enough to get the full match means:
options: Turning down part of your salary package permanently
Better cash flow with no cost
questions.explanation: Employer matching is an instant return; capture the full match before other savings.

questions.question: A pension is different from a savings account because:
options: Money is invested for the long term and usually locked until pension age
questions.explanation: Pensions trade access for tax relief and long-term growth; keep emergency money separate.

questions.question: The State Pension requires:
options: Enough qualifying years of National Insurance contributions or credits, usually 35 for the full amount
questions.explanation: Around 35 qualifying years gets the full new State Pension; check your forecast online.

questions.question: You can check your State Pension forecast and NI record:
options: Free online via the government's State Pension forecast service
questions.explanation: The gov.uk forecast tool shows what you'd get and any gaps to fill.

questions.question: The State Pension age is currently:
options: Rising to 67, with further rises legislated
questions.explanation: State Pension age is increasing to 67 and later 68 depending on birth date; check your own date.

questions.question: Pensions from old employers can be located via:
options: The government's Pension Tracing Service, free
questions.explanation: The free tracing service finds contact details for lost pensions; consolidation is a separate decision.

questions.question: Before consolidating old pensions, check:
options: Exit fees, fund quality and any guarantees you'd lose
Only the color of the app
questions.explanation: Lost guarantees or high exit fees can outweigh simpler admin; compare before merging.

questions.question: Pension money is normally inaccessible until:
options: Age 55, rising to 57 from 2028 (dates can change)
questions.explanation: Normal minimum pension age is 55, rising to 57 in 2028; special cases exist.

questions.question: A pension 'drawdown' means:
options: Leaving money invested and taking income from it flexibly
questions.explanation: Drawdown keeps investments growing while you take income; annuities buy guaranteed income instead.

questions.question: Pension scammers often promise:
options: Guaranteed high returns, early access, or 'free pension reviews' out of the blue
questions.explanation: Cold calls about pensions are illegal; hang up and use regulated advisers only.

questions.question: A LISA versus a pension for retirement savings:
options: LISAs suit some basic-rate savers; pensions usually win with employer contributions or higher-rate relief
questions.explanation: Employer match and tax relief usually favour pensions; LISAs add flexibility for first homes.

questions.question: Annual allowance for pension contributions is roughly:
options: £60,000 (can change, tapered for very high earners)
questions.explanation: Most people can contribute up to £60,000 a year with relief; very high incomes taper it.

questions.question: The earlier you start pension contributions, the more you benefit from:
options: Decades of compounding, so small early amounts beat big late ones
questions.explanation: £50 a month from 25 can beat £200 a month from 45, purely through time.

questions.question: Self-employed people building a pension typically use:
options: A personal pension or SIPP with tax relief
questions.explanation: SIPPs and personal pensions give self-employed workers the same relief and compounding.

questions.question: If you die before drawing your pension, it generally:
options: Can pass to beneficiaries, often tax-free if you die before 75 (rules are nuanced)
questions.explanation: Pension death benefit rules are favourable but complex; nominate beneficiaries with your provider.

questions.question: Pension contributions reduce the take-home pay cut because of tax relief: contributing £80 net can mean £100 invested for a basic-rate taxpayer, so the real cost of £100 saved is:
questions.explanation: That's relief in action: £80 out of your net pay becomes £100 in the pension.

questions.question: The State Pension is paid:
options: Weekly, for life, once you reach State Pension age
questions.explanation: It's a regular lifetime income, which is why NI years are valuable.

questions.question: Checking your payslip for pension contributions shows:
options: Whether you're enrolled, how much goes in, and whether employer money is included
questions.explanation: Read the payslip: verify you're in the scheme and the contributions match what was promised.
